ranked_results.content: Pre-trained language model representations have been successful in a wide range of language understanding tasks. In this paper, we examine different strategies to integrate pre-trained representations into sequence to sequence models and apply it to neural machine translation and abstractive summarization. We find that pre-trained representations are most effective when added to the encoder network which slows inference by only 14%. Our experiments in machine translation show gains of up to 5.3 BLEU in a simulated resource-poor setup. While returns diminish with more labeled data, we still observe improvements when millions of sentence-pairs are available. Finally, on abstractive summarization we achieve a new state of the art on the full text version of CNN/DailyMail.

ranked_results.content: We presented an analysis of different strategies to add pre-trained language model representations to sequence to sequence models for neural machine translation and abstractive document summarization. Adding pre-trained representations is very effective for the encoder network and while returns diminish when more labeled data becomes available, we still observe improvements when millions of examples are available. In future research we will investigate ways to improve the decoder with pre-trained representations.

ranked_results.content:
Here is a comprehensive, detailed summary of the paper, including all key details:

---

**Title Implied**: *Integrating Pre-Trained Language Model Representations into Sequence-to-Sequence Models for Neural Machine Translation and Abstractive Summarization*

---

### **Core Objective**
The paper investigates how to effectively integrate pre-trained language model (LM) representations into sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) architectures for two language generation tasks: **neural machine translation (NMT)** and **abstractive summarization**. The goal is to leverage the rich, context-aware representations from large-scale pre-trained LMs to improve performance — especially in low-resource settings — while minimizing computational overhead. ---

### **Background & Motivation**
- Pre-trained LMs (e.g., BERT, ELMo) have shown significant gains in language understanding tasks by transferring knowledge from massive unlabeled corpora to downstream tasks with limited labeled data. - Prior work has explored integrating LMs into Seq2Seq models, primarily in the **decoder** (e.g., ELMo-style embeddings before the decoder output), but not extensively for **text generation**. - In NMT, some work has focused on transferring representations across language pairs (high-resource → low-resource), but not for generation tasks. - The paper aims to fill this gap by evaluating multiple integration strategies across both NMT and abstractive summarization. ---

### **Key Contributions**
1. **Comprehensive Study of Integration Strategies**:
   - Evaluate multiple ways to inject pre-trained LM representations into Seq2Seq models:
     - **ELMo-style contextualized embeddings** (input to encoder/decoder)
     - **Fine-tuning the LM** (adjusting LM parameters during Seq2Seq training)
     - **Tying encoder/decoder embeddings** (shared word representations)
   - Compare performance across **varying amounts of labeled data** (simulated resource-poor to resource-rich settings). 2. **Best Performing Strategy**:
   - **Inputting ELMo-style representations into the encoder** yields the best results. - This strategy is **computationally efficient** — inference is only **12–14% slower** than baseline, due to parallelizable LM computation. - Adding **shared decoder embeddings** further boosts performance. 3. **Performance Gains**:
   - **NMT (WMT’18 en-de)**:
     - Up to **+5.3 BLEU** in simulated low-resource settings (160K sentence-pairs). - Gains diminish with more data, but still **+1+ BLEU** even at 5.2M sentence-pairs. - **Abstractive Summarization (CNN/DailyMail)**:
     - Achieves **new state-of-the-art** on full-text version using a **bi-directional LM** augmented encoder. - Evaluated using **F1-Rouge** (Rouge-1, Rouge-2, Rouge-L). 4. **Model Architecture & Training Details**:
   - **LMs**: Trained on **6B+ tokens** (German: 260M sentences, English: 193M sentences). - **Vocabulary**: Joint BPE vocab of **37K types** (for en-de), **32K types** for summarization. - **Seq2Seq Models**: Based on **Transformer architecture** (Big Transformer for NMT, base Transformer for summarization). - **Training**:
     - Optimizer: **Adam** with learning rate schedule (linear warm-up → cosine decay to 0.0001). - Dropout: Tuned between 0.1–0.4. - Label smoothing with uniform prior. - Training on **32–8 GPUs**, using **16-bit floating point**. - Training time: 6 days (bi-directional LM), 4 days (uni-directional LM). 5. **Data & Evaluation**:
   - **NMT**:
     - **WMT’18 en-de**: 5.18M sentence-pairs (filtered for length ratio ≤1.5). - **WMT’18 en-tr**: 208K sentence-pairs (no filtering). - Evaluated on **case-sensitive de-tokenized BLEU**. - **Summarization**:
     - **CNN/DailyMail**: 280K articles with multi-sentence summaries. - Articles truncated to **400 tokens**. - Evaluated on **F1-Rouge**. - **Baseline**: Strong transformer model. - **Comparison**: Against BIBREF26 (task-specific architecture) — pre-trained representations are **complementary**. 6. **Implementation Details**:
   - **ELMo-style Integration**:
     - Linear combination of LM layers:  
       `ELMo = Σ(α_i * LM_layer_i)`, where α_i are learned scalars, normalized to sum to 1. - Layer normalization applied before ELMo computation. - **Fine-tuning LM**:
     - Replace encoder input embeddings with LM layer outputs (before softmax). - Add dropout to LM output. - Tune number of encoder blocks (found critical for performance). - **Decoder Integration**:
     - Similar to encoder, but less effective — gains diminish or vanish with more data. - **Decoder Embedding Sharing**:
     - Tying input/output embeddings improves performance significantly. 7. **Computational Trade-offs**:
   - **Training Speed**:
     - Adding LM representations slows training throughput by **5.3x** (ELMo) to **9.2x** (fine-tuning). - **Inference Speed**:
     - Encoder-based ELMo: **12–14% slower** (parallelizable). - Decoder-based: Much slower (sequential LM calls — not cached). - **Future Work**: Cache LM operations to speed up inference. 8.

ranked_results.content: We consider two benchmarks: Most experiments are run on the WMT'18 English-German (en-de) news translation task and we validate our findings on the WMT'18 English-Turkish (en-tr) news task. For WMT'18 English-German, the training corpus consists of all available bitext excluding the ParaCrawl corpus and we remove sentences longer than 250 tokens as well as sentence-pairs with a source/target length ratio exceeding 1.5. This results in 5.18M sentence pairs. We tokenize all data with the Moses tokenizer BIBREF8 and apply the BPE vocabulary learned on the monolingual corpora.

ranked_results.content: Our experiments rely on strong transformer-based language models trained on up to six billion tokens (§ SECREF3 ). We present a detailed study of various strategies in different simulated labeled training data scenarios and observe the largest improvements in low-resource settings but gains of over 1 BLEU are still possible when five million sentence-pairs are available. The most successful strategy to integrate pre-trained representations is as input to the encoder network (§ SECREF4 ).

ranked_results.content: Pre-training of language models has been shown to provide large improvements for a range of language understanding tasks BIBREF0 , BIBREF1 , BIBREF2 , BIBREF3 . The key idea is to train a large generative model on vast corpora and use the resulting representations on tasks for which only limited amounts of labeled data is available. Pre-training of sequence to sequence models has been previously investigated for text classification BIBREF4 but not for text generation. In neural machine translation, there has been work on transferring representations from high-resource language pairs to low-resource settings BIBREF5 .
